title: Job 34:31–37
context: Elihu closes this part of his speech by modeling a prayer of repentance and urging Job to respond, then charging that Job speaks without knowledge and adds rebellion to his sin. These are Elihu’s arguments, reported rather than rubber-stamped: the LORD later speaks of words without knowledge (38:2), yet also says Job spoke of him what is right, unlike the three friends (42:7). Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about humility before God, without declaring a verdict on Elihu.

verses.text: “For has any said to God, ‘I am guilty, but I will not offend any more.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu asks whether anyone has said to God, ‘I am guilty, but I will not offend any more.’ Elihu models a confession.

Arminian readers see repentance as a real, freely offered response to God.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse is difficult, and interpreters differ on whether Elihu offers a model for Job or asks a general question.

Reformed readers see a call to humility before God. Both traditions read this as shared ground about repentance, without assuming Job’s guilt.

verses.text: Teach me that which I don’t see. If I have done iniquity, I will do it no more’?
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu continues the imagined prayer: ‘Teach me that which I don’t see. If I have done iniquity, I will do it no more.’ Humility is modeled.

Arminian readers see a teachable spirit offered to God.
verses.reformedNotes:
The prayer asks God to reveal hidden faults, a request that suits any believer.

Reformed readers see humble dependence on God for self-knowledge. Both traditions read this as shared ground about teachability and the desire to turn from sin.

verses.text: Shall his recompense be as you desire, that you refuse it? For you must choose, and not I. Therefore speak what you know.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu asks whether God should repay on Job’s terms, since Job refuses; Job must choose and say what he knows. He challenges Job.

Arminian readers see a call for Job to respond for himself.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse is among the most difficult in the chapter, and its exact sense is debated.

Reformed readers see Elihu insisting that God’s recompense is not set by human preference. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hold the meaning tentatively.

verses.text: Men of understanding will tell me, yes, every wise man who hears me:
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu says men of understanding and every wise listener will agree with him. He appeals to the judgment of others.

Arminian readers note that the appeal does not settle whether Elihu is right; readers must still weigh his claims.
verses.reformedNotes:
Elihu expects the wise to confirm his verdict on Job in verse 35.

Reformed readers see an appeal to consensus that must be tested against the whole book. Both traditions read this as shared ground and do not treat the appeal as a final verdict.

verses.text: ‘Job speaks without knowledge. His words are without wisdom.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu imagines the wise saying, ‘Job speaks without knowledge. His words are without wisdom.’ The verdict is sharp.

Arminian readers weigh it as Elihu’s argument, not the book’s settled verdict.
verses.reformedNotes:
The LORD later asks, “Who is this who darkens counsel by words without knowledge?” (38:2), and Job admits speaking of things he did not understand (42:3). Yet 42:7 commends Job over the friends.

Reformed readers likewise weigh it. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: I wish that Job were tried to the end, because of his answering like wicked men.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu wishes Job would be tried to the end, because he answers like wicked men. The wish is severe.

Arminian readers see a harsh wish that sits uneasily with the prologue’s portrait of Job (1:8).
verses.reformedNotes:
Elihu’s wish may express a desire for Job to be fully tested and corrected, though its tone is hard.

Reformed readers see sharp words that readers must weigh against the book’s ending. Both traditions read this as shared ground and report Elihu’s wish without endorsing it.

verses.text: For he adds rebellion to his sin. He claps his hands among us, and multiplies his words against God.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu says Job adds rebellion to his sin, claps his hands mockingly, and multiplies words against God. The chapter ends in accusation.

Arminian readers report this as Elihu’s charge, not a verdict the book confirms.
verses.reformedNotes:
In 42:7 the LORD says Job spoke of him what is right, in contrast with the three friends, though Elihu is not named there.

Reformed readers likewise weigh the charge. Both traditions read this as shared ground and declare no verdict on Elihu.
